prime.problem: Expanding around every centre finds the longest palindrome in O(n²), and on inputs like "aaaa…" it really does 1,000,000 checks for n = 1,000. Neighbouring centres re-verify the same characters because nothing remembers what an earlier palindrome already proved.
prime.fits: Third Strings card. Like KMP, it reuses information instead of re-reading characters, with a pointer that only moves right. Its radius array also answers the palindromic-prefix question KMP solved for Shortest Palindrome.
expect: # separators: every palindrome gets one centre
prime.goal: Trace the radius array with mirror head starts, explain the three mirror cases, and prove the algorithm is linear.

attend: Why does inserting # make even-length palindromes like "abba" work with the same loop as odd ones?
Inside the rightmost palindrome, why does position i see the same surroundings as its mirror 2c − i, reversed?
Why must the head start be clipped to r − i, as at i = 7 of "babad"?
When the mirror's palindrome fits strictly inside, why is the one check guaranteed to fail?
Why do successful checks total at most about 2n over the whole run?

must: Inside the rightmost-reaching palindrome (c, r), the text around i mirrors the text around j = 2c − i → i's radius is at least min(r − i, p[j]) for free → only characters beyond r need comparing

Three cases: mirror fits strictly inside → p[i] = p[j], one failing check; mirror touches or passes r → start at r − i and expand past r → every successful check moves r right, and r never moves left → at most 2n successes + 2n + 1 failures → O(n) (1,999 checks on "a" × 1,000 vs 1,000,000)

p[i] in the # string = the palindrome's length in s, starting at (i − p[i]) / 2 → the radius at every centre, not only the longest → counts all palindromic substrings (Σ (p + 1) // 2) and finds the longest palindromic prefix
elevated: The # transform doubles the string to 2n + 1 → one loop, no odd/even special cases → the source's radius-array version avoids building t by treating even positions as implicit separators
reference: Manacher's 1975 JACM paper title and original purpose

compress.prompt: In 3–4 sentences from memory: what the # string and radius array are, what (c, r) remembers, how the mirror gives a head start, and why r moving only right makes it linear.
checklist: t = # + joined letters + #; p[i] = radius in t = length in s
(c, r): the palindrome reaching furthest right so far
inside it, start p[i] at min(r − i, p[2c − i]); outside, at 0
only expand past r; each success pushes r right
O(n) total; gives every centre's radius

retrieve.q: Explain why the mirror position's radius is a safe lower bound for i's radius only up to r − i, and not beyond.
answer: inside c's palindrome, the characters around i equal those around j, reversed
beyond r nothing is known yet, so the mirror's longer radius may not hold there
hence min(r − i, p[j]); anything past r must be checked

retrieve.q: Walk through i = 5 in "#b#a#b#a#d#" (c = 3, r = 6 before the step): the mirror, the head start, the checks and the new (c, r).
answer: mirror j = 2·3 − 5 = 1, p[1] = 1; start = min(6 − 5, 1) = 1 (touches r)
p[5] = 3 ("aba"), and r moves to 8: (c, r) = (5, 8)

retrieve.q: Interview question: longest palindromic substring, n ≤ 1,000, no adversarial input. Manacher or expand-around-centre? When would your answer flip?
answer: expand-around-centre: shorter and hard to get wrong; O(n²) only bites on long palindromic runs
Manacher: O(n) always, but more index bookkeeping
flip to Manacher for large n, adversarial input like "aaaa…", or when you need every centre's radius (counting palindromes)

compare.q: Manacher finds palindromic substrings in O(n); palindrome-partitioning DP uses an O(n²) is-palindrome table. What does each compute, and could Manacher's radii replace the table?
answer: Manacher: the maximal radius at every centre
the DP table: whether each s[i..j] is a palindrome, for every pair
yes for the check: s[i..j] is a palindrome iff its centre's radius covers it, an O(1) test after O(n) preprocessing; the partition DP itself stays O(n²)

compare.q: Both KMP and Manacher can give the longest palindromic prefix (Shortest Palindrome). How does each get it, and which extra answers does each structure give you?
answer: KMP: last lps value of s + # + reverse(s)
Manacher: the largest p[i] with i − p[i] = 0
KMP's table also gives periods and pattern matches; Manacher's radii give every palindrome, e.g. the count of palindromic substrings

predict.q: For s = "aaaa", predict the radius array (9 entries) and the number of palindromic substrings. Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: p = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0]. The centre # at index 4 has radius 4 (the whole string). Count = Σ (x + 1) // 2 = 0 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 10: four "a", three "aa", two "aaa", one "aaaa".

apply.task: Run Manacher by hand on abaaba: build t, then fill p[i] for i = 0 … 12, writing for each the mirror, the head start and the (c, r) after. Read off the longest palindrome and the count of palindromic substrings.
apply.done: p = [0, 1, 0, 3, 0, 1, 6, 1, 0, 3, 0, 1, 0]; the longest is the whole string abaaba (p[6] = 6, centred between the two a's); the count is 11.
apply.hint: At i = 9 the mirror is j = 2·6 − 9 = 3 with p[3] = 3, and r − i = 12 − 9 = 3: a head start of 3, and no further check is possible because the palindrome already touches the end of t.
